questions.q: A 40,000 wspm leading-edge fab cost $20 billion and depreciates its tools over 5 years. If utilization falls from 90% to 50%, what happens to the depreciation cost per wafer, and why does this matter for foundry behavior?
options: It roughly doubles (from ~$8k to ~$14k per wafer), which is why foundries discount older nodes to keep fabs loaded rather than idle them
It stays the same because depreciation is a fixed cost that does not depend on output
It falls, because fewer wafers mean less tool wear and lower maintenance
It rises by about 10%, a minor effect compared with materials costs
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation (~$3.4B) is fixed, so spreading it over 240,000 instead of 432,000 wafers raises the per-wafer charge from ~$7,900 to ~$14,200. This operating leverage is why utilization, not price, drives foundry margins through the cycle.

questions.q: Why has cost per transistor stopped falling meaningfully since roughly the 28 nm node, even though logic density still improves ~1.5–1.7x per node?
options: Because foundries now use only EUV, which makes every layer more expensive than DUV
Because wafer price rises ~1.5–1.8x per node, SRAM bit cells stopped shrinking (N3E ~0.021 um^2, same as N5), and analog/I/O do not scale, so most of the die does not get cheaper
Because transistor counts have hit the reticle limit and can no longer grow
Because design costs are now included in wafer prices by the foundries
questions.explanation: Wafer price growth now cancels the density gain, and roughly half the area of a modern CPU or GPU (SRAM, analog, I/O) barely scales at all, which is why chiplets moved those blocks to older nodes.

questions.q: The October 2023 update to the US export controls replaced the interconnect-bandwidth test of the October 2022 rule with a performance-density metric. What loophole did that close?
options: Chinese firms had been buying EUV scanners through Singapore intermediaries
NVIDIA had built the A800 and H800 by capping interconnect bandwidth at 400 GB/s on otherwise identical dies, keeping them under the 600 GB/s threshold while retaining full compute
Hyperscalers had been renting H100 capacity to Chinese customers from data centers in Malaysia
SMIC had been importing immersion DUV tools classified as 28 nm equipment
questions.explanation: The 2022 rule caught chips with TPP >= 4800 and interconnect >= 600 GB/s; A800/H800 ducked the second test. The 2023 rule keys on TPP and TPP per mm^2 alone, which is what forced the far weaker H20 (TPP ~2400).

questions.q: What is the binding technical limit on SMIC's ability to follow TSMC below 5 nm-class, given that it has demonstrated 7 nm-class (Kirin 9000S, 2023) and 5 nm-class parts?
options: China cannot obtain 300 mm silicon wafers of sufficient purity
SMIC lacks EDA tools capable of place-and-route below 7 nm

Without EUV, each shrink requires more DUV multi-patterning passes, so mask count, cost, and defect exposure rise while yield falls (reported well below 50% at 5 nm-class), making the node possible but uneconomic and 3 nm-class not credible
SMIC's fabs are limited to 200 mm wafers
questions.explanation: EUV has never been licensed to China and immersion DUV above the NXT:1980i class is now restricted, so SMIC's only path is quadruple-plus patterning, which trades yield and cost for dimension.

questions.q: Roughly what fraction of the world's most advanced (5 nm-class and below) logic wafers and of CoWoS-class advanced packaging is produced in Taiwan, and which risk scenario would most directly remove that output without physically damaging fabs?
options: About 50% of both; a major earthquake near Tainan
About 90% of both; a naval blockade that stops inbound chemicals, gases and spares and outbound wafers within weeks
About 70% of wafers and 30% of packaging; a US export-control action against TSMC
About 90% of wafers but under 20% of packaging; a typhoon season power outage
questions.explanation: Taiwan holds ~90% of leading-edge logic and ~90%+ of CoWoS-class packaging. Fabs hold days to weeks of consumables, so a blockade idles them without destroying them; earthquakes such as Hualien (Apr 2024) have cost only ~0.1% of a quarter's revenue.

questions.q: The CHIPS Act's Section 48D investment tax credit was raised from 25% to 35% in the July 2025 tax law. In the worked example of moving ~12,500 wspm of N3 capacity to Arizona, what is the net effect of US incentives on capex versus Taiwan, and where does the persistent US cost penalty actually sit?
options: Net US capex is still ~50% above Taiwan because tools cost more in the US; the penalty is tool pricing

Net US capex ends up below Taiwan's unsubsidized figure because tools (~80% of capex) cost the same everywhere and the credit plus grants offset the ~1.5x construction premium; the persistent penalty is ~5–20% higher operating cost per wafer
Incentives exactly cancel the construction premium, leaving costs identical; the penalty is entirely in mask-set costs
Incentives do not apply to foreign-headquartered firms like TSMC, so the full 1.5x premium remains
questions.explanation: Only the ~20% building share carries the construction premium; the 35% credit on qualifying property and pro-rata grants more than offset it. The lasting gap is per-wafer operating cost (labor, imported chemicals, scale), which TSMC recovers by pricing US-origin wafers higher.

questions.q: Under the October 2023 US export rule, total processing performance (TPP) is peak operations per second in trillions multiplied by the bit-width of those operations, and performance density is TPP divided by die area. An H100 delivers ~989 TFLOPS of dense 16-bit math on an 814 mm^2 die; the H20 uses the same die at ~148 TFLOPS. Which statement is correct?
options: H100: TPP ~15,800 and density ~19 TPP/mm^2, over both the 4,800 and 5.92 lines; H20: TPP ~2,370 and density ~2.9, under the control lines and just under the 2,400 notification band, which is why it was exportable
Both chips have the same TPP because they share a die; only interconnect bandwidth differs
H20 fails the density test because it uses the full 814 mm^2 die
TPP is measured in memory bandwidth, so the H20 with full HBM3 is controlled and the H100 is not
questions.explanation: TPP = ~989 x 16 = ~15,800 for H100 (density ~15,800 / 814 = ~19 TPP/mm^2); TPP = ~148 x 16 = ~2,370 for H20 (density ~2.9). The H20 keeps H100 memory but ~15% of its compute, which is why it was designed to sit just under the 2,400 band.

questions.q: Roughly 6 million Blackwell-class packages a year each carry two ~800 mm^2 compute dies (about 60 usable dies per 300 mm wafer), one CoWoS interposer (~15-20 packages per CoWoS wafer), and 8 HBM stacks of 12 DRAM dies. Which part of the chain does this demand strain most, given TSMC shipped ~15 million wafers in 2025 and CoWoS capacity was ~70,000-75,000 wafers a month at the end of 2025?
options: Front-end logic wafers: ~200,000 N4 wafers a year is most of TSMC output

CoWoS and HBM: the compute dies need only ~200,000 wafers a year (~1-2% of TSMC output), but the packages need ~350,000 CoWoS wafers (a third to a half of capacity) and ~600 million leading-edge DRAM dies at 2-3x the wafer area per bit of commodity DRAM
Photomasks: each package needs a new mask set
Nothing is strained; all three lines have spare capacity
questions.explanation: 12 million dies / 60 per wafer = ~200,000 wafers = ~17,000 wspm, ~1-2% of TSMC. 6 million packages / ~17 per CoWoS wafer = ~350,000 CoWoS wafers = ~30,000 wpm against ~70,000-75,000. 48 million stacks x 12 dies = ~600 million HBM dies from 1-beta/1-gamma lines, which is why CoWoS and HBM, not front-end wafers, were the bottlenecks.
